title: Structure-Based Drug Design
summary: Using 3D structures of targets to design drugs.

lessons.title: Protein structures: X-ray, cryo-EM, prediction

levels.kid: Proteins are tiny machines in our body, folded into special shapes. To design a medicine that fits a protein, scientists want to see its shape, like seeing the shape of a lock before making a key. There are three main ways. **X-ray crystallography** turns proteins into tiny crystals and shines X-rays at them to work out the shape. **Cryo-EM** freezes proteins super cold and takes thousands of pictures with a special microscope, then joins them into one 3D picture. And now, smart **computer programs** like AlphaFold can guess a protein's shape just from its recipe. The guesses are often very good, but scientists still double-check.
levels.hs:
**Structure-based drug design (SBDD)** uses the 3D shape of a target protein to design drugs that fit it. There are three main ways to get that shape.

- **X-ray crystallography**: scientists grow crystals of the protein, often with a drug bound, and fire X-rays at them. The way the X-rays scatter is used to calculate an **electron density map**, and a model of the atoms is fitted into it. Resolution is measured in ångströms (Å); smaller numbers mean sharper detail. Around 2 Å or better shows atoms clearly.
- **Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM)**: proteins are frozen quickly in thin ice and imaged many thousands of times with an electron microscope. Computers combine the images into a 3D map. Cryo-EM is great for big complexes and membrane proteins (like many receptors) that are hard to crystallize.
- **Structure prediction**: AI programs such as **AlphaFold** predict a protein's 3D structure from its amino acid sequence. They are very accurate for many proteins and come with a confidence score for each part.

Each method has limits. Crystals can force unnatural shapes; cryo-EM maps can be blurry in places; predictions may get details wrong in drug-binding pockets. Scientists check structures carefully before using them to design drugs. Most structures are shared publicly in the **Protein Data Bank (PDB)**.
levels.college:
SBDD depends on accurate, relevant target structures. Each source has characteristic strengths and quality indicators.

**X-ray crystallography**: diffraction from protein crystals yields structure-factor amplitudes; phases come from molecular replacement or experimental methods. Key quality metrics: **resolution** (lower is better; ligand placement is usually reliable at about 2.5 Å or better), **R-work/R-free** (agreement between model and data; R-free uses withheld reflections to avoid overfitting), **B-factors** (atomic displacement, indicating mobility or disorder), and **occupancy**. Always inspect the ligand's fit to the electron density (2Fo−Fc and Fo−Fc maps) rather than trusting the model blindly. Crystallography gives the highest throughput for ligand complexes, enabling routine iterative SBDD.

**Cryo-EM**: single-particle analysis averages images of many particles. Since direct electron detectors (around 2013), near-atomic resolution has become common, revolutionizing structures of membrane proteins (GPCRs, ion channels, transporters) and large complexes without crystallization. Local resolution varies; flexible regions and small ligands can be poorly defined. Smaller proteins (below roughly 50 kDa) remain challenging.

**Predicted structures**: AlphaFold2 (2020) achieved accuracy competitive with experiment for many single-domain proteins; its developers shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with David Baker. Per-residue confidence (pLDDT) and predicted aligned error indicate reliability. Limitations for drug design: side-chain conformations in pockets, ligand-induced changes, multiple conformational states, and cofactors or ligands that are absent. Newer models predict protein–ligand complexes, but their poses require validation.

**NMR** can also determine structures of smaller proteins in solution and probe dynamics.

Good practice: use the highest-quality relevant structure (ideally with a ligand bound in the same pocket), check for missing loops, crystal contacts and protonation states, and prepare the structure (add hydrogens, assign tautomers) before modeling.
levels.phd:
A structure is a model fitted to data, and its usefulness for design depends on how faithfully it represents the conformational ensemble relevant to binding.

In crystallography, the electron density is an average over billions of molecules and the exposure time; alternative conformations, partial ligand occupancy and disorder are compressed into one model with B-factors. Ligand misplacement, unjustified ligands modeled into weak density and incorrect tautomers or ring flips have been documented in public structures. Validation tools (real-space correlation coefficients, density fit metrics, geometry checks) help identify unreliable ligands. Cryo-cooling can bias side-chain and water distributions; room-temperature crystallography reveals conformational heterogeneity masked at 100 K, sometimes changing interpretation of a binding site.

Cryo-EM reconstructions vary locally in resolution because of flexibility and heterogeneity. Classification can separate conformational states, enabling structure-based design against specific states (for example, active versus inactive GPCRs, or particular ion channel states). Map sharpening and model building at moderate resolution can introduce errors in side-chain placement, which matters for ligand design.

Deep-learning structure prediction learns coevolutionary and structural regularities. It is typically excellent at backbone folds but can predict a single dominant state, often resembling the apo or most commonly crystallized conformation. Cryptic pockets that open only upon ligand binding, induced-fit changes and allosteric sites may be missed. Benchmarks show docking into predicted structures can underperform docking into holo crystal structures, though performance improves with refinement or ensemble generation. Co-folding models that predict ligand complexes may memorize training examples and can produce physically implausible interactions for novel chemotypes, so physics-based checks remain important.

The practical synthesis is an ensemble view: combining experimental structures, predicted models and molecular dynamics to represent plausible binding-site states rather than relying on one static picture.
levels.expert:
Senior structural and computational chemists approach every structure with healthy skepticism.

Practical checks before designing from a structure:
- **Look at the density, not just the model.** Open the electron density or cryo-EM map around the ligand and key residues. If the ligand's density is weak or broken, its pose may be partly guessed.
- **Check resolution and local quality.** A 1.8 Å crystal structure supports detailed hydrogen-bond analysis; a 3.5 Å cryo-EM map may not resolve side chains or waters in the pocket.
- **Prefer holo structures.** A structure with a similar ligand bound captures induced-fit changes. Apo structures and predictions can show a collapsed or different pocket.
- **Mind crystal contacts and constructs.** Truncated constructs, stabilizing mutations, or crystal packing can distort a site. Compare multiple structures if available.
- **Use predicted structures wisely.** AlphaFold models are excellent for planning when no experimental structure exists, but low-confidence regions and pocket side chains need caution. Validate key design hypotheses experimentally.
- **Assign protonation and tautomers carefully.** Histidines, aspartates near ligands and ligand tautomers change hydrogen-bond patterns.

Pitfalls: designing around a water that is not really there, trusting a ligand modeled into noise, and assuming one structure represents all relevant states. Experienced teams also remember that structures show where a molecule binds, but not always how tightly, or how it behaves in cells. Structure is a guide for hypotheses, which the DMTA cycle then tests.

keyPoints: SBDD uses 3D target structures to design drugs.
X-ray crystallography gives electron density maps; lower resolution numbers mean more detail.
Cryo-EM excels for large complexes and membrane proteins.
AI predictions (AlphaFold) are powerful but less reliable for pocket details and induced fit.
Always check the experimental density and structure quality.

lessons.title: Reading a binding site

levels.kid: A binding site is a little pocket on a protein where a medicine can sit. Scientists look closely at the pocket to see what it likes. Some spots in the pocket are greasy and like greasy parts of a medicine. Some spots love to hold hands using tiny links called **hydrogen bonds**. Some spots are charged, like magnets, and pull on opposite charges. There might even be little water molecules sitting inside. Reading a pocket is like looking at a glove before choosing a hand. When the medicine's shape and its sticky spots match the pocket, it holds on tight.
levels.hs:
A **binding site** is the pocket or groove where a drug attaches to its target. To design a drug that fits, chemists "read" the site's shape and chemistry.

Key interactions they look for:
- **Hydrogen bonds**: an H attached to N or O (a donor) is attracted to a lone pair on N or O (an acceptor). These give direction and specificity.
- **Hydrophobic contacts**: greasy parts of the drug pack against greasy amino acids like leucine, valine and phenylalanine. This releases ordered water and provides a lot of binding strength.
- **Ionic interactions (salt bridges)**: a positively charged group, like a protonated amine, pairs with a negatively charged aspartate or glutamate.
- **π-stacking and cation–π**: flat aromatic rings stack together, or a positive charge sits over an aromatic ring.
- **Metal coordination**: some enzymes have a metal ion (like zinc) that drugs can bind.

Chemists also note:
- **Water molecules**: some are tightly bound and can bridge the drug and protein; others can be pushed out to gain strength.
- **Flexibility**: pockets can change shape when a drug binds (induced fit).
- **Shape and size**: is the pocket deep and enclosed (easier to target) or flat and open (harder)?

Understanding these features helps chemists decide where to add a group, which direction to grow, and what to avoid.
levels.college:
Reading a binding site means analyzing its geometry, chemistry, solvation and dynamics to generate design hypotheses.

**Geometry and druggability**: deep, enclosed, mostly hydrophobic pockets with some polar anchors tend to bind small molecules with high affinity. Shallow, polar or highly flexible sites (many protein–protein interfaces) are harder. Pocket-detection algorithms (fpocket, SiteMap) estimate volume, enclosure and hydrophobicity to give druggability scores.

**Interactions**:
- Hydrogen bonds: optimal donor–acceptor distances are roughly 2.7–3.2 Å with near-linear geometry; backbone NH and C=O groups are frequent partners (for example, the kinase hinge).
- Hydrophobic contacts and the hydrophobic effect: burying nonpolar surface releases ordered water, often driving affinity.
- Salt bridges: strong in buried environments but weakened by solvent exposure and desolvation costs.
- Aromatic interactions: edge-to-face and offset stacking; cation–π with Trp, Tyr, Phe.
- Halogen bonds: a σ-hole on Cl, Br or I interacts with a Lewis base such as a carbonyl oxygen.
- Metal coordination: zinc in metalloproteases and carbonic anhydrases; magnesium in many nucleotide sites.

**Water**: conserved, well-ordered waters mediate interactions and may be retained in design. Displacing a high-energy (poorly hydrogen-bonded) water can boost affinity. Computational tools estimate water energetics.

**Flexibility**: induced fit, conformational selection and cryptic pockets mean one structure may not show every possibility. Comparing multiple ligand-bound structures reveals flexible regions.

**Selectivity**: comparing the site with close homologs (for example, other kinases) highlights residues that differ, such as gatekeeper residues, which designers exploit for selectivity.

**Solvent-exposed regions**: groups pointing to solvent tolerate polar substituents that improve properties without losing affinity.
levels.phd:
Binding-site analysis aims to infer which features contribute most to binding free energy and how they can be exploited, recognizing that structure alone does not reveal energetics.

Hot spots, a minority of residues contributing most of the binding energy, are often enriched in Trp, Tyr and Arg and located in partially enclosed, hydrophobic regions. Alanine scanning, fragment mapping and computational solvent mapping converge on these regions, which helps prioritize design efforts.

Desolvation shapes interaction energetics. A hydrogen bond formed in the binding site replaces hydrogen bonds each partner made with water, so its net contribution can be small or even unfavorable unless geometry is excellent or the site is shielded from solvent. Buried, unpaired polar groups are especially costly. Thus, gains from polar interactions depend on context, while hydrophobic burial gives relatively reliable but property-costly affinity.

Water thermodynamics vary widely. Inhomogeneous solvation theory and related methods estimate enthalpy and entropy of hydration sites; waters in hydrophobic enclosures with few hydrogen bonds are thermodynamically unfavorable and attractive targets for displacement. Conversely, waters with strong networks contribute to stability, and displacement may be penalized unless the ligand replaces their interactions.

Electrostatics extend beyond local contacts: long-range fields, pKa shifts of ionizable residues and ligands upon binding (buried environments can shift pKa values markedly), and protonation-state changes affect affinity and its pH dependence.

Conformational ensembles complicate a single-structure view. Ligands may bind rare conformations (conformational selection) whose population cost reduces apparent affinity. Cryptic pockets, revealed by molecular dynamics or by ligand binding, offer opportunities for allosteric or selective inhibitors. Integrating structural, thermodynamic and dynamic information yields more reliable design hypotheses than inspecting static contacts.
levels.expert:
Experienced designers read a binding site with a checklist and a sense of what is cheap versus costly to change.

Practical approach:
- **Identify the anchors.** Which interactions are conserved across all potent ligands? Hinge hydrogen bonds in kinases, a salt bridge to an aspartate in aminergic GPCRs, or zinc binding in metalloenzymes. Keep these intact.
- **Map the sub-pockets.** Note empty regions near the ligand that could be filled, and their character (greasy, polar, charged).
- **Find the solvent-exposed vector.** This is where you add solubilizing or property-tuning groups without hurting binding.
- **Examine waters carefully.** Conserved bridging waters can be kept; isolated waters in greasy pockets are candidates for displacement. Check whether waters are well defined in density.
- **Compare with off-targets.** Overlay homolog structures to spot residues unique to your target, such as a small gatekeeper, a different loop, or a distinct charge, and design to exploit them.
- **Respect flexibility.** If a loop or side chain moves between structures, design for the range, and test hypotheses in multiple structures.
- **Check protonation states.** Histidines, buried acids and ligand amines may change charge in the site.

Pitfalls: chasing an apparent hydrogen bond that costs more desolvation than it gains, filling a pocket with lipophilic groups that inflate logD, ignoring selectivity until late, and over-trusting one crystal structure. Senior designers turn site reading into explicit hypotheses ("adding a nitrile here should engage that backbone NH and improve selectivity over the homolog") and test them quickly.

keyPoints: Binding sites are read for shape, chemistry, water and flexibility.
Key interactions: hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, salt bridges, aromatic and halogen bonds, metal coordination.
Displacing an unhappy water can boost affinity; conserved waters may be kept.
Solvent-exposed vectors are good places to tune properties.
Comparing with homologs reveals selectivity opportunities.

lessons.title: Docking & scoring

levels.kid: Docking is a computer game for scientists. They give the computer the shape of a protein pocket and a molecule. The computer tries to fit the molecule into the pocket in lots of different ways, twisting and turning it, like trying to fit a puzzle piece. Then it gives each try a **score** for how well it fits. The best scores are the computer's guesses for how the molecule sits. Scientists can even dock millions of molecules to find a few that might work. But the computer's scores are only guesses, so scientists must test the best ones in the real lab.
levels.hs:
**Molecular docking** is a computer method that predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein's binding site and estimates how well it binds.

Docking has two parts:
1. **Search (pose prediction)**: the program tries many positions, orientations and conformations (twists) of the molecule inside the pocket.
2. **Scoring**: each pose gets a score based on interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts and clashes. The best-scoring pose is the predicted binding mode.

Docking is used in two main ways:
- **Pose prediction**: to understand how a known active molecule binds, helping chemists design improvements.
- **Virtual screening**: docking huge libraries (now even billions of molecules) to pick a small number for testing.

Docking is useful but limited. Scoring functions are simplified, so scores often do not match true binding strength well. Programs usually treat the protein as rigid, ignore some water effects, and can miss induced fit. A docking pose is a hypothesis, not proof. Chemists check that poses make chemical sense, compare with crystal structures when possible, and test docking hits in real assays.

Common docking programs include AutoDock Vina, Glide and GOLD.
levels.college:
Docking predicts ligand binding modes and ranks compounds using approximate scoring functions.

**Search algorithms** explore ligand translational, rotational and torsional degrees of freedom (and sometimes limited receptor flexibility): systematic/incremental construction, Monte Carlo, genetic algorithms, and gradient-based optimization. Receptor flexibility is handled through side-chain sampling, induced-fit protocols, or docking into ensembles of structures.

**Scoring functions**:
- *Force-field based*: van der Waals and electrostatic terms, sometimes with implicit solvation.
- *Empirical*: weighted terms (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contact, rotatable-bond penalty) fitted to measured affinities (for example, Glide and Vina-like functions).
- *Knowledge-based*: statistical potentials derived from atom-pair frequencies in known complexes.
- *Machine-learning*: models trained on structures and affinities; powerful but risk learning dataset biases.

**Performance**: pose prediction succeeds often (a pose within 2 Å RMSD of the crystal pose is the usual criterion), especially when the receptor structure came from a similar ligand complex (redocking or cross-docking). Affinity ranking across diverse compounds is weak; correlations with measured affinity are typically modest.

**Virtual screening**: success is measured by **enrichment**, how many more actives appear in the top-ranked fraction compared with random selection. Benchmarks use known actives mixed with decoys. Ultra-large docking campaigns of hundreds of millions to billions of make-on-demand molecules have found potent, novel ligands for targets including GPCRs and enzymes.

**Best practices**: prepare the protein (protonation, waters, missing atoms), validate by redocking known ligands, use pharmacophore or interaction constraints, visually inspect top poses, and rescore or cluster to diversify picks. Always confirm hits experimentally with dose-response and orthogonal binding methods.
levels.phd:
Docking approximates a statistical-mechanical problem: computing the binding free energy, which depends on an ensemble of bound and unbound states, solvent reorganization and conformational entropy. Most scoring functions instead evaluate a single pose with additive pairwise terms, so their failure to rank affinities is structural rather than a matter of parameter tuning.

Key approximations include: rigid or minimally flexible receptors; implicit or neglected solvent, so desolvation and water-mediated interactions are poorly treated; neglect of ligand strain and conformational entropy beyond simple rotatable-bond penalties; and inaccurate electrostatics in heterogeneous dielectric environments. Scoring functions trained on affinity datasets also learn correlations with molecular size, so larger molecules tend to score better, a bias that complicates virtual screening and inflates apparent enrichment.

Ultra-large library docking changes the statistics. As libraries grow to billions of molecules, the absolute number of molecules that score well by chance also grows, and rare scoring artifacts (molecules exploiting weaknesses of the function) can dominate the top ranks. Yet prospective studies showed hit rates and potencies improving with library size, suggesting the true actives also become more numerous. Selecting diverse, chemically sensible compounds from top ranks, often by expert inspection, remains important.

Machine-learning scoring and deep-learning docking or co-folding methods can reproduce crystallographic poses on benchmarks, but analyses reveal sensitivity to data leakage (similar proteins or ligands across training and test sets) and frequent physically implausible poses with steric clashes or impossible geometry. Physics-based validity checks and prospective testing are essential for fair evaluation.

Docking is thus best viewed as a filter that enriches, followed by more rigorous methods (free-energy calculations, experimental testing) for prioritization.
levels.expert:
Experienced computational chemists use docking as a hypothesis generator and enrichment tool, not an oracle.

Practical guidance:
- **Validate the setup first.** Redock known ligands and, ideally, run a retrospective enrichment test with known actives and decoys. If the setup cannot reproduce known binders, prospective results will be unreliable.
- **Choose the right structure.** A holo structure with a chemically similar ligand usually docks better than an apo or predicted structure. Consider docking to several structures.
- **Handle waters and protonation deliberately.** Keep conserved bridging waters, remove questionable ones, and test both choices if unsure. Assign histidine states and ligand charges carefully.
- **Use constraints from knowledge.** If every known ligand makes a hinge hydrogen bond, require it. This removes many nonsense poses.
- **Look at the poses.** Visual inspection catches unrealistic strain, buried unpaired polar groups and odd tautomers that scores miss.
- **Do not rank by score alone.** Cluster top hits by chemotype, filter for properties and interference motifs, and pick diverse compounds.
- **Treat scores as weak affinity predictors.** Within a congeneric series, docking may suggest which pose is right, but free-energy methods or experiments should rank potency.

Pitfalls: overinterpreting tiny score differences, ignoring size bias, docking into a pocket that does not exist in solution, and reporting virtual "hits" without experimental confirmation. Good teams also feed experimental results back into the docking setup to refine it over time.

keyPoints: Docking predicts how a molecule sits in a pocket (pose) and scores its fit.
Search algorithms explore positions and conformations; scoring functions rank poses.
Pose prediction often works; affinity ranking is weak.
Virtual screening success is measured by enrichment of actives.
Docking hits must be confirmed experimentally.

lessons.title: Free-energy calculations

levels.kid: Sometimes chemists want to know which of two molecules will stick better before they make them. Making molecules takes a long time, so they ask the computer first. The computer pretends to slowly change one molecule into the other, a tiny bit at a time, like a magic shape-shifting trick. It does this once inside the protein pocket and once floating in water. By comparing the two, it figures out which molecule holds on tighter. This is called a **free-energy calculation**. It takes a lot of computer power, but it is often a pretty good guess. That helps chemists choose the best molecules to make.
levels.hs:
Docking scores are fast but rough. When chemists need a more accurate prediction of how tightly a molecule binds, they can use **free-energy calculations**.

**Binding free energy (ΔG)** measures how strongly a drug binds. More negative means tighter binding. A difference of about 1.4 kcal/mol corresponds to roughly a tenfold change in binding strength at body-like temperature.

The most common method in drug design is **relative binding free energy (RBFE)**, often done with **free energy perturbation (FEP)**. Instead of calculating the binding of each molecule from scratch, the computer "alchemically" transforms molecule A into a closely related molecule B in small steps. This is done twice: once with the molecule bound to the protein, and once in water. The difference tells whether B binds better or worse than A.

These simulations use **molecular dynamics**, which moves every atom according to physics, including the surrounding water. That is why they are far more expensive than docking, but also more accurate. Good FEP predictions are often within about 1 kcal/mol of experiment.

Chemists use FEP to rank design ideas before synthesis, saving time. It works best for small changes in a series where a good crystal structure is available.
levels.college:
Free-energy calculations estimate binding affinities using physics-based simulations with explicit solvent.

**Thermodynamic basis**: ΔG_bind = −RT ln(K_A); at 298 K, a tenfold change in affinity corresponds to about 1.36 kcal/mol. Because free energy is a state function, alchemical paths that do not occur physically can still yield correct differences.

**Relative binding free energy (RBFE)** uses a thermodynamic cycle. Ligand A is transformed into ligand B in the bound state (ΔG_complex) and in solution (ΔG_solvent). Then ΔΔG_bind = ΔG_complex − ΔG_solvent. Transformations proceed through intermediate λ windows, with soft-core potentials to avoid singularities when atoms appear or disappear. Free energies are computed by free energy perturbation (FEP), thermodynamic integration (TI) or Bennett acceptance ratio methods.

**Performance**: in prospective industrial use with well-prepared systems, RBFE often achieves root-mean-square errors of around 1 kcal/mol and useful ranking for congeneric series. Accuracy depends on force field quality, adequate sampling, correct protonation and tautomer states, and a reliable starting structure.

**Absolute binding free energy (ABFE)** decouples the whole ligand from its environment, often with restraints. It can compare dissimilar compounds but is more expensive and noisier.

**Cheaper end-point methods**, such as MM-PBSA and MM-GBSA, estimate binding energy from snapshots of bound and unbound states. They are faster but less accurate, best used for qualitative ranking.

**Challenging cases**: changes in net charge, ring opening or scaffold changes, large conformational rearrangements, flexible loops, buried water rearrangement and metal-containing sites. Workflows use perturbation maps linking many ligands, cycle closure checks and reference compounds with known affinity to detect errors.
levels.phd:
Alchemical free-energy methods rest on statistical mechanics: the free-energy difference between two Hamiltonians can be computed from ensemble averages, as in Zwanzig's exponential averaging (FEP) or Kirkwood's thermodynamic integration. Practical estimators such as the multistate Bennett acceptance ratio (MBAR) use data from all λ windows and give minimum-variance estimates.

The main error sources are force-field inaccuracy and incomplete sampling. Fixed-charge force fields neglect electronic polarization, which matters for charged and highly polar systems; torsional parameters for drug-like molecules are frequently refined with quantum calculations. Sampling problems arise when the bound ligand or protein has slow degrees of freedom, such as side-chain rotamers, loop motions, alternative binding modes or water exchange between buried sites and bulk. Enhanced sampling techniques (replica exchange with solute tempering, grand canonical water sampling) reduce these issues.

Charge-changing perturbations introduce finite-size and periodic electrostatic artifacts requiring corrections or co-alchemical counterions. Protonation-state changes on binding couple binding to pH, and multiple states may need explicit treatment and weighting.

Statistical validation distinguishes real predictive power from overfitting to retrospective benchmarks. Errors of around 1 kcal/mol correspond to roughly fivefold affinity error, so FEP is most useful for prioritization: it reduces the number of compounds synthesized by discarding designs predicted to lose activity, rather than pinpointing exact potencies. Retrospective success can be inflated by selecting favorable systems; prospective blinded assessments give more realistic accuracy.

Emerging directions include machine-learned force fields and potentials trained on quantum data, combining active learning with FEP to explore larger design spaces, and absolute methods for scaffold hopping and selectivity prediction across related proteins.
levels.expert:
In a project team, free-energy calculations are a tool for deciding what to make next, and their value depends on careful setup and honest validation.

Practical habits:
- **Validate retrospectively first.** Run FEP on 10 to 20 compounds already measured in the series. If predictions do not track the data within about 1 kcal/mol, fix the setup before trusting prospective results.
- **Start from a reliable binding mode.** A crystal structure with a closely related ligand is ideal. If the pose is uncertain, run calculations for alternative poses.
- **Get protonation and tautomers right.** A wrong charge on a ligand or a histidine can ruin predictions.
- **Use FEP for congeneric series.** Small substituent changes, ring swaps and modest core modifications work best. Large scaffold hops, charge changes and big flexibility changes need extra care.
- **Watch for sampling warnings.** Poor overlap between λ windows, large cycle closure errors and inconsistent replicate results signal trouble.
- **Combine with chemistry judgment.** Use FEP to filter out likely losers and to prioritize among synthetically feasible ideas, not to replace chemical intuition or ADMET considerations.

Pitfalls: believing a predicted 0.3 kcal/mol advantage is meaningful, running FEP without experimental anchors, and ignoring that predicted potency is only one parameter in multiparameter optimization. Well-run teams track prospective accuracy over time, so they know when the method is helping their specific target and when it is not.

keyPoints: Free-energy calculations predict binding affinity using physics-based simulations.
About 1.36 kcal/mol equals a tenfold affinity change at 298 K.
Relative binding free energy uses a thermodynamic cycle and alchemical transformations.
Good FEP often reaches about 1 kcal/mol error for congeneric series.
Charge changes, scaffold hops and slow motions are hard cases.

lessons.title: Case study: HIV protease inhibitors

levels.kid: HIV is a virus that attacks the body's defenders. To make new copies of itself, HIV uses a pair of tiny scissors called **HIV protease**. The scissors cut long virus chains into working pieces. Scientists took detailed pictures of these scissors and saw exactly what they looked like, even a little flap that closes like a lid. Then they designed medicines that fit right into the scissors and jam them, so they can't cut. These medicines, called **protease inhibitors**, were some of the first medicines designed using pictures of their target. Taken with other HIV medicines, they helped turn HIV from a deadly illness into one people can live with.
levels.hs:
**HIV protease** is an enzyme the virus needs to mature. It cuts long viral protein chains (Gag and Gag-Pol) into working proteins. Without it, new virus particles are not infectious.

In 1989, scientists solved the crystal structure of HIV protease. It turned out to be a **symmetrical dimer**: two identical halves, each contributing one aspartic acid to the active site. Two flexible "flaps" close over the substrate like a lid. Knowing this shape let chemists design drugs to fit.

The key idea was to mimic the **transition state**, the unstable shape the substrate takes while being cut. Chemists replaced the cuttable bond with a non-cuttable group containing a hydroxyl that binds the two aspartic acids. This makes the drug a tight-binding blocker.

The first protease inhibitor, **saquinavir**, was approved in 1995, followed by ritonavir and indinavir in 1996. Combined with other HIV drugs in "combination therapy," they dramatically reduced HIV deaths.

Problems included poor absorption and fast breakdown by liver enzymes. Ritonavir turned out to be a strong blocker of the liver enzyme CYP3A4, so it is now used mostly as a "booster" that keeps other protease inhibitors in the blood longer. Later drugs like **darunavir** were designed to bind tightly to the enzyme's backbone so they stay effective when the virus mutates.
levels.college:
HIV-1 protease inhibitors are a landmark of structure-based drug design.

**Target**: HIV-1 protease is a C2-symmetric homodimeric aspartyl protease (99 residues per monomer) with catalytic Asp25 and Asp25′. Flexible β-hairpin flaps close over the substrate. A conserved structural water molecule bridges the flaps (Ile50/Ile50′) and the substrate or inhibitor carbonyls. The enzyme cleaves Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins, including at Phe–Pro and Tyr–Pro junctions that human aspartyl proteases rarely cleave, aiding selectivity.

**Design strategy**: peptidomimetic transition-state isosteres replace the scissile amide with non-hydrolyzable groups, such as hydroxyethylamine (saquinavir) or hydroxyethylene, whose secondary hydroxyl hydrogen-bonds both catalytic aspartates. Side chains fill the S1/S1′ and S2/S2′ subsites. Crystal structures of enzyme–inhibitor complexes guided iterative optimization.

**Drugs and timeline**: saquinavir (1995), ritonavir and indinavir (1996), nelfinavir (1997), followed by amprenavir, lopinavir, atazanavir, tipranavir (a non-peptidic inhibitor) and darunavir (2006). Their introduction into combination antiretroviral therapy (from 1996) caused dramatic falls in AIDS mortality.

**Challenges and solutions**:
- *Poor oral bioavailability and rapid CYP3A4 metabolism* of peptidomimetics. Ritonavir, a potent mechanism-based CYP3A4 inhibitor, is used as a pharmacokinetic booster (as in lopinavir/ritonavir). Cobicistat is a booster without antiviral activity.
- *Resistance*: mutations in the active site and flaps reduce binding. Darunavir's bis-tetrahydrofuran group forms hydrogen bonds with backbone atoms (Asp29, Asp30), which cannot change by mutation, giving a high genetic barrier to resistance.
- *Adverse effects*: metabolic effects such as dyslipidemia and insulin resistance, gastrointestinal effects, drug–drug interactions, and indinavir-associated kidney stones.

DuPont Merck's cyclic ureas showed that designing a group to displace the flap water could produce potent inhibitors, an influential concept even though those compounds did not become marketed drugs.
levels.phd:
HIV protease inhibitor discovery illustrates how structural, mechanistic and evolutionary insight interact in drug design.

Mechanistically, the aspartyl protease activates a water molecule between Asp25 and Asp25′ for nucleophilic attack on the scissile carbonyl, producing a tetrahedral gem-diol intermediate. Hydroxyethylamine and hydroxyethylene isosteres mimic this tetrahedral geometry, positioning a hydroxyl between the aspartates. The extent of protonation of the catalytic dyad, inferred by NMR and neutron crystallography in some complexes, affects how inhibitors engage the site and influences computational modeling.

Structural water was a central theme. The flap water bridges inhibitor carbonyls and Ile50/Ile50′ backbone amides. The DuPont Merck cyclic urea design replaced this water with a urea carbonyl, gaining entropy from water release and preorganizing the inhibitor, a frequently cited example of rational water displacement.

Resistance evolution shaped later design. Mutations at active-site residues (for example V82A, I84V) and distal positions (L90M, flap changes) reduce inhibitor binding while preserving substrate processing. The "substrate envelope" hypothesis proposed that inhibitors protruding beyond the volume occupied by natural substrates are more vulnerable, because mutations at those contact points spare substrate recognition. Inhibitors fitting within the envelope, and those relying on backbone hydrogen bonds, as with darunavir's bis-THF ligand, retain potency against many resistant variants. Darunavir also shows very slow dissociation and may inhibit protease dimerization.

The pharmacokinetic story is equally instructive. Ritonavir's mechanism-based inhibition of CYP3A4 turned a liability into a strategy, establishing pharmacokinetic boosting and inspiring cobicistat. Boosting raises trough concentrations, helping suppress resistant virus, but magnifies drug–drug interactions, a major clinical consideration.

Together, these lessons influenced later design of inhibitors for HCV protease and SARS-CoV-2 main protease, including the use of ritonavir boosting with nirmatrelvir.
levels.expert:
HIV protease inhibitors offer lessons that experienced drug hunters and clinicians still use.

For drug designers:
- **Exploit symmetry and mechanism.** The C2-symmetric active site and the aspartate dyad suggested transition-state mimics positioned between the catalytic residues. Understanding the mechanism gave a strong starting hypothesis.
- **Design for resistance from the start.** Viruses mutate quickly. Binding to conserved backbone atoms and staying within the substrate envelope makes resistance harder, as darunavir shows.
- **Think about water.** Structural waters can be retained or displaced deliberately. Displacement can pay off, but only when the replacing group recreates the water's interactions.
- **Do not ignore pharmacokinetics.** Peptide-like inhibitors were potent but poorly absorbed and quickly metabolized. Boosting rescued them, but at the cost of interaction complexity. Modern programs try to build good PK into the molecule.

For clinicians:
- **Boosted protease inhibitors interact with many drugs.** Ritonavir and cobicistat strongly inhibit CYP3A4, raising levels of statins, some sedatives, certain antiarrhythmics and many others. Always check an interaction database before adding any medicine.
- **Combination therapy is essential.** Protease inhibitors are used with other antiretroviral classes to prevent resistance.
- **Monitor metabolic and organ effects.** Watch lipids, glucose, liver tests and, for atazanavir, harmless but noticeable bilirubin rises.
- **Know the barrier to resistance.** Darunavir-based regimens are valued for their high genetic barrier.

The broader legacy is that structure-guided design, combined with an understanding of resistance and pharmacokinetics, can deliver drugs that change the course of a pandemic disease.

Inhibitors mimic the tetrahedral transition state with a hydroxyl between the aspartates.
Saquinavir (1995) was first; combination therapy cut AIDS deaths dramatically.
Ritonavir is now used mainly as a CYP3A4 'booster'.
Darunavir binds backbone atoms, giving a high barrier to resistance.
